#table(stroke: none, columns: 6, align: (left, left, left, left, left, left, ), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 0), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 1), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 2), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 3), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 4), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 5), table.vline(stroke: .5pt, x: 6), table.hline(stroke: .5pt), [$t$ (hours)], [0], [0.3], [1.7], [2.8], [4], table.hline(stroke: .5pt), [$v_(P)(t)$ (meters per hour)], [0], [55], [-29], [55], [48], table.hline(stroke: .5pt));

The velocity of a particle, $P$, moving along the $x$-axis is given by the differentiable function $v_(P)$, where $v_(P)(t)$ is measured in meters per hour and $t$ is measured in hours. Selected values of $v_(P)(t)$ are shown in the table above. Particle $P$ is at the origin at time $t = 0$.

(a) Justify why there must be at least one time $t$, for $0.3 <= t <= 2.8$, at which $v_(P) ""^(prime)(t)$, the acceleration of particle $P$, equals 0 meters per hour per hour.

(b) Use a trapezoidal sum with the three subintervals \[0, 0.3\], \[0.3, 1.7\], and \[1.7, 2.8\] to approximate the value of $integral_(0)^(2.8) v_(P)(t) d t$.

(c) A second particle, $Q$, also moves along the $x$-axis so that its velocity for $0 <= t <= 4$ is given by $v_(Q)(t)= 45 sqrt(t) cos lr((0.063 t^(2)))$ meters per hour. Find the time interval during which the velocity of particle $Q$ is at least 60 meters per hour. Find the distance traveled by particle $Q$ during the interval when the velocity of particle $Q$ is at least 60 meters per hour.

(d) At time $t = 0$, particle $Q$ is at position $x = - 90$. Using the result from part (b) and the function $v_(Q)$ from part (c), approximate the distance between particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t = 2.8$.
